title: Hanyang: Capital Relocation, Urban Planning, and Sacred Geography
description: Hanyang reveals how a dynasty turned landscape into government and government into urban space.

blocks.title: Choosing a political center
paragraphs: A new dynasty needed a place from which to govern, but a capital was far more than a convenient headquarters. It housed officials, ritual sites, stores, workshops, military facilities, markets, and the residences of people whose labor sustained the court. Choosing a city meant imagining how a new political order should appear in space. Early Joseon’s move toward Hanyang was therefore an act of state-making as well as urban planning.

The location offered geographical advantages, yet the arguments for it also drew upon ideas about auspicious setting, defensibility, access, and centrality. It is tempting to read later city growth backward and treat the eventual capital as the only possible choice. At the time, alternatives and disagreements formed part of the process.

blocks.title: Palace, gates, and streets
paragraphs: A planned royal capital makes power visible. The position of gates, major roads, palace compounds, state offices, and ritual buildings tells people where authority is located and how it expects the city to function. Such arrangements are not merely aesthetic. They affect movement, access to officials, patterns of commerce, and the daily journeys of workers who keep a city operating.

The ideal city described in planning language could never perfectly predict the city people actually inhabited. Population changes, household needs, fires, repairs, and commerce continually altered the built environment. The physical capital was both a political statement and a changing urban organism.

blocks.title: Work behind the royal city
paragraphs: Palaces do not construct themselves. Building and maintaining an urban center required timber, stone, transport, food supply, skilled craftspeople, and large numbers of laborers. These needs connected the new capital to the countryside and to river routes. A capital concentrates resources, making its apparent grandeur inseparable from the wider economy that sustains it.

Markets and neighborhoods grew within an administrative landscape. A person working as a merchant, porter, craftsperson, or servant encountered the royal city from a very different angle than a court official entering an audience hall. Both experiences belong in the history of Hanyang.

blocks.title: The afterlife of a foundation
paragraphs: Over time, the city became layered with memories of reform, conflict, occupation, modernization, and growth. Later Seoul cannot simply be equated with early Joseon Hanyang, but its historical geography provides a powerful way to trace continuities and ruptures. Streets and landmarks carry names whose meanings shift across centuries.

Studying the founding capital opens routes into architecture, ritual government, rivers and transport, urban everyday life, and the changing political geography of Korea. The story is not only that a ruler chose a city; it is that generations of people continuously remade it.

blocks.title: The old capital and the problem of political distance
paragraphs: The decision to relocate the court from the Gaegyeong region was entangled with the memory of Goryeo institutions and the political relationships concentrated there. Moving a government could weaken particular networks while giving the new dynasty a chance to design the geography of administrative authority. It was neither a purely aesthetic preference nor simply the consequence of a geomantic prediction.

A capital needed accessible roads, water, fields capable of feeding a large population and space for royal ritual. Hanyang's position along the Han River corridor offered advantages for transport and connections to inland production. Yet those features did not erase debate about building costs and security. The existence of alternatives reminds readers that later Seoul's importance should not make its founding location appear predestined.

blocks.title: Competing proposals and the choice of site
paragraphs: Accounts of the early 1390s preserve discussion of possible locations for the royal centre. Court officials weighed practical and symbolic considerations, including terrain, ancestral ritual and the relation between palace precincts and surrounding mountains. Those categories were not mutually exclusive: views about auspiciousness could be intertwined with assessments of water, defence and the prestige of a ruling house.

A historian should distinguish a decision recorded in an annal from explanations attributed to particular advisors in later writing. Detailed stories of individual geomancers have often grown in retelling; they are not necessarily direct evidence of every survey conducted. The firmer historical point is that a new court brought administrative ambition to a contested landscape and then committed enormous resources to transforming it.

blocks.title: Jongmyo and Sajik: ritual foundations of government
paragraphs: Royal ancestral rites and sacrifices for earth and grain gave the capital an institutional sacred geography. The placement of Jongmyo, the royal ancestral shrine, and Sajik, the state altars, articulated relationships between dynastic continuity, land and proper government. These were not optional ornaments added after politics had been settled. They helped define what a legitimate royal capital ought to contain.

Ritual space also required recurring labor, officials, offerings and maintenance. A ceremonial plan could therefore shape budgets and the movements of people throughout the year. The meaning of a shrine cannot be separated from administrative routines through which rites were carried out. Nor does the existence of Confucian state rites mean Buddhist devotion or older local practices disappeared from the lives of capital residents.

blocks.title: Gyeongbokgung and the architectural hierarchy
paragraphs: The principal palace precinct made the distinction between monarch, advisors and service personnel visible in space. Gates, courts and halls organized audience, state documents and ceremonial access. Constructing these settings helped institutionalize a new monarchy, giving ministers and envoys recognizable places within its hierarchy.

The built result should not be imagined as identical to every later version of Gyeongbokgung. Fires, wars and major reconstructions transformed buildings over centuries. Surviving complexes and plans preserve valuable evidence only when dated carefully. The politics of early Joseon construction is best studied through accounts of initial works, later alterations and the tasks that required constant repair, rather than through a photograph of the palace today.

blocks.title: Walls, gates and labour behind urban order
paragraphs: The city walls and gates defined controlled approaches to the royal centre, but they also demanded large mobilizations of labor and materials. Quarrying, timber transport, roadmaking and provisioning connected the capital project to people living far beyond its walls. Work obligations could impose costs on cultivators even if the finished infrastructure served public security.

Official descriptions of successful construction typically foreground the monarch's determination and ministers' planning. A social history asks who transported stone, where food was supplied and how seasonal labour affected household farming. The archival traces of these groups are limited, yet their work was indispensable. Urban grandeur and rural burdens were parts of the same historical process.

blocks.title: Markets, neighbourhoods and the inhabited city
paragraphs: Royal officials required food, clothing, tools and domestic services, creating opportunities for merchants, artisans and transport workers. Commercial activity developed within a city whose street network also reflected administrative priorities. A centre planned for the throne became an everyday environment with private calculations and competing demands for space.

Residents were not passive occupants of a perfectly fixed diagram. Houses changed hands, workshops appeared, fires required rebuilding and trade connected the capital to river landings and rural markets. Regulations attempted to organize these activities, but their effect varied over time. The distinction between ideal urban design and lived settlement prevents architectural history from excluding the majority who kept the city functioning.

blocks.title: Geomancy without reductionism
paragraphs: Ideas about mountains, water and auspicious placement belonged to the intellectual vocabulary of court planners. They can illuminate why certain sites were debated and how rulers sought to show that the new dynasty fitted a morally ordered landscape. Yet presenting geomancy as a substitute for material considerations creates a false opposition.

A mountain might possess cosmological significance while also offering defence or shaping roads. Officials could argue through multiple frameworks at once. Conversely, a modern geographical explanation should not erase the historical actors' own religious and philosophical language. The historian's task is to identify the beliefs documented in a particular source and examine their relationship to administrative choices, not to invent a single secret reason for the city's selection.

blocks.title: From founding ambition to the lived capital
paragraphs: Hanyang's political role eventually survived the founding dynasty's early succession violence and periods of royal absence. Its endurance reflects sustained investment in roads, markets, ritual buildings and government offices, not simply the wisdom of one initial choice. The return and stabilisation of the court after early disruptions demonstrate that the capital was created through repeated decisions.

The city's history became much longer than Taejo's reign. Subsequent generations altered its water supply, walls and institutions while attaching new memories to old places. A source-critical foundation narrative should hold the 1390s in their own uncertainty and then explain how later developments made Hanyang durable. That approach makes the capital a historical process rather than an inevitable destination.
